Permits & Regulations

Demolishing for Renovation and Additions

Permits, protocols, and preparation homeowners should know before demolition begins on a Toronto tear-down, renovation, or addition.

Updated for 2026 · 5 min read

Book Consultation

In This Guide

  • Full Home Demolition
  • Demolition for Renovation
  • Demolition for Additions
  • Utilities & Disconnections
  • Heritage & Zoning
  • Waste Removal & Salvage
  • Timelines
  • Costs
  • Choosing the Right Path

Demolition is one of the earliest and most misunderstood phases of a construction project. Whether you're rebuilding a new home, opening up an existing layout, or preparing for a home addition, demolition sets the stage for everything that comes after — framing, mechanicals, inspections, and finishes.

In Toronto, demolition also comes with permit requirements, safety protocols, environmental rules, and coordination with utilities, the City, and trades.

Full Home Demolition (Tear-Down & Rebuild)

Full demolition means removing the entire existing structure down to the foundation, or in many cases, including the foundation itself if the new build requires re-engineering. Common reasons homeowners choose a full tear-down:

  • Aging home with structural issues.
  • Modern energy standards not met — an envelope upgrade is impossible.
  • Rebuilding larger under current zoning.
  • Higher long-term ROI vs. renovating.
  • Custom home build opportunity.

This is the path chosen for many older Toronto bungalows, wartime homes, and small detached homes in neighbourhoods like Ledbury Park, East York, Scarborough, Bedford Park, and parts of Etobicoke.

In Toronto, full residential demolition requires a Residential Demolition Permit – With Replacement Building and often a simultaneous building permit for the replacement home. The City checks for heritage property status, tree protection zones, gas/hydro/water disconnections, replacement dwelling plans, and waste disposal approach.

Demolition for Home Renovation (Partial Structural / Interior)

Renovation demolition focuses on removing parts of the home to update or reconfigure it — not tearing down the entire structure. Common renovation demolition scenarios include removing load-bearing walls for open-concept layouts, removing old kitchens and bathrooms, stripping back to studs for a full renovation, removing outdated finishes, insulation and wiring, floor removal, basement underpin prep, and removing chimney stacks or fireplaces.

Contrary to belief, partial demolition often requires a permit, especially if any structural element is altered, including load-bearing walls, roof framing, structural beams or joists, foundation modifications, and stair opening modifications. The relevant rule is under the Building Code: see the City's When Do I Need a Building Permit? guidance. Interior non-structural demo, such as removing cabinets or flooring, usually does not require a permit, but homeowners frequently over-assume this.

Older Toronto homes may contain asbestos (vinyl tiles, insulation, plaster, duct wrap), lead paint, knob-and-tube wiring, mould, or vermiculite. Professional abatement may be required before demolition begins.

Demolition for Home Additions (Rear, Second Storey, Side)

Demolition for additions is a hybrid category — you're not tearing down the whole house, but you're removing structural elements to extend the home. Common types of additions in Toronto include a rear addition (most common), a second-storey addition or "top-up" on a bungalow, a side addition when zoning setbacks allow, a front addition (rare but possible), and an underpin plus basement addition that adds living area.

Demolition scope typically includes removing existing exterior walls, removing roofing or roof trusses, cutting and removing foundations or slabs, removing decks or outbuildings in the footprint, and removing interior structure where tied in. All additions require a building permit, which covers structural demolition, structural tie-in to the existing home, new foundation work, and envelope and mechanical systems — see the City's Building Permit Requirements. If trees are impacted within protected distances, a Tree & Ravine Protection Permit may also be required.

Utilities & Disconnections

Before any demolition, utilities must be safely shut down or temporarily capped, depending on the scope:

  • Hydro (Toronto Hydro) — disconnect or temporary power.
  • Gas (Enbridge) — disconnect or lock-off.
  • Water (City of Toronto) — shut-off or temporary bypass.

Heritage & Zone Considerations

Toronto has strict rules for heritage-designated homes, heritage conservation districts, neighbourhood character retention, and lot coverage, FSI, and setbacks. See the City's heritage approvals guidance when applicable.

Waste Removal & Salvage

Modern demolition includes concrete and asphalt recycling, metal recycling, wood reuse, abatement waste containment, and salvage of architectural items. Many Toronto homeowners now salvage brick, hardwood flooring, kitchen cabinetry, trimwork, and doors and hardware.

Timelines

Typical timelines:

ScopeTimeline
Full tear-down1–3 days (after permits)
Renovation demo3–10 days
Addition demo5–20 days
Permit approvals2–12+ weeks
Utility disconnection4–10 weeks

Note: permitting is usually longer than demolition itself.

Costs (High-Level)

Approximate ballpark ranges in Toronto:

ScopeCost Range
Full home demolition$18,000 – $45,000+
Renovation demo$5,000 – $35,000+
Addition demo$8,000 – $60,000+
Abatement (if required)$3,000 – $25,000+
Permit/utility fees$500 – $4,500+

Actual costs vary based on house size, access, waste volume, hazardous materials, foundation removal, dump fees, and protection requirements.

When Homeowners Choose Each Path

ScenarioBest Option
Old bungalow, want more spaceTear-down + custom build
Same footprint, better interiorRenovation demo
Need more floor areaAddition demo
Raising ceiling / adding heightSecond-storey addition
Want modern floor planRenovation + structural demo

Demolition isn't just destruction — it's a highly coordinated part of construction involving permits, engineering, safety, environmental factors, utilities, inspections, logistics, and planning. Choosing the right demolition scope ensures the next phase — framing, mechanicals, finishing — runs smoothly and legally.

If you're looking to demolish, build, renovate, or add, consult with an experienced, HCRA-licensed design-build team before work begins.
